beginner.headline: SpaceX Catches Starship’s Top Part for the First Time
beginner.brief: SpaceX caught the top part of its Starship rocket for the first time. The flight lasted twenty-two and a half hours. The top part travelled around Earth 14 times before coming back. The launch tower’s arms caught it when it returned to Earth. Workers cheered as the rocket returned to the launch area in Texas. SpaceX also wanted to catch the bottom part, but this did not happen. The bottom part went to the ocean and exploded. SpaceX wants to use both parts again to make flights cost less.

intermediate.headline: SpaceX Catches Starship’s Upper Section for the First Time
intermediate.brief: SpaceX has recovered the upper section of its Starship rocket for the first time after a journey lasting twenty-two and a half hours. Near the launch tower, it was secured by mechanical arms nicknamed chopsticks. The company also planned to catch the lower section, but cancelled this attempt a few minutes after launch. The lower section, called the Super Heavy booster, was due to return six and a half minutes after launch. However, the booster automatically changed direction towards the ocean, hovered above the water and then exploded. The upper section deployed 26 satellites that are part of Starlink, a system providing high-speed internet. It completed 14 orbits, or full journeys around Earth, before returning to the launch tower. SpaceX wants both sections to be reusable, meaning they can be used for future flights. Recovering both sections reliably would allow SpaceX to launch Starship repeatedly and greatly reduce costs. The company had already caught the booster on three earlier test flights. Before the flight, SpaceX said it would try to catch the upper section only after carefully assessing its condition in space.

advanced.headline: SpaceX Catches Starship’s Upper Stage in Recovery Breakthrough
advanced.brief: SpaceX recovered Starship’s upper stage for the first time after a flight lasting twenty-two and a half hours. The returning vehicle hovered beside its launch tower before enormous mechanical arms, nicknamed chopsticks, gripped it. The booster triggered an automated abort, a cancellation initiated by its own systems, before diverting to the ocean, hovering above the water and exploding. During its journey into space, the upper stage released 26 satellites belonging to the Starlink constellation, a satellite system providing high-speed internet. The Ship completed fourteen circuits of Earth before returning to the launch tower. Before launch, SpaceX said an effort to catch the Ship would be contingent on a careful assessment of the vehicle in space. Had problems emerged, the Ship would have been brought down in the ocean instead. Developing a fully reusable rocket remains a long-held ambition for SpaceX. The company needs dependable recovery of both Starship sections to enable repeated flights and sharply lower costs. Falcon 9 already illustrates the financial value of partial reuse: its rockets fly more than 100 times annually, and reusing the lower section has substantially reduced launch costs. SpaceX had already caught the Super Heavy booster on three earlier test flights. Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of the Royal Aeronautical Society, said landing an entire Starship would represent a major advance in spaceflight. In his assessment, the next milestone is to combine the two recovery achievements in one flight and demonstrate that the process works dependably, repeatedly and economically. Starship’s progress has direct implications for Nasa’s ambition to land humans on the Moon in 2028, a highly ambitious timetable. SpaceX’s Nasa contract requires it to configure the Ship as a lander that will eventually carry astronauts to the lunar surface. Starship’s development has proceeded more slowly than SpaceX intended, and considerable progress in the coming months is necessary to meet its commitments.
